passage:
At Dadaji's flat, Anand hung back by the door.
“Anand, greet Dadaji,” said Disha, his mother.
“Do I have to touch his feet?”
“Only if you want to. You can also fold your hands and say namaste.”
Dadaji chuckled from his chair. “A warm hello is enough, beta. Come here.”
Anand looked at the floor, then walked over and bent to touch Dadaji's feet. Dadaji put a hand lightly on his head. “Blessings. How is school?”
“Good,” said Anand, smiling. “I got a star.”

qa.q: Who told Anand he could fold his hands instead of touching feet?
qa.a: Disha, his mother, told him he could fold his hands and say namaste.

qa.q: What might Anand have felt when he hung back and asked if he had to touch feet, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably shy or unsure about the custom, and perhaps a little pressured. He might also just have been nervous about meeting Dadaji.

qa.q: How did the adults respond in a way that respects the child?
qa.a: Disha and Dadaji made it a choice, saying a warm hello is enough, so Anand touched the feet by his own decision.

qa.q: How might Dadaji see the touching of his feet?
qa.a: As a mark of respect and a chance to bless his grandchild, and he also said a warm hello would do, so he did not seem to demand it.

grounding: Touching elders' feet is respect and a way to receive blessings, and a child is never forced into touch.

passage: I'm Suraj. Every morning I touch my grandfather's feet. It's my way of saying thank you, and he blesses me. When my friend Wasim came over, he greeted my grandmother by putting a hand on his chest and saying, “Assalamu alaikum.” She smiled and said “Wa alaikum assalam.” Then she asked, “May I bless you too?” Wasim nodded, and she touched his head gently. Later she told me, “Respect lives in the heart, not only in the feet.” I thought about that. Wasim's way and mine are different, and both are respectful.

qa.q: What does Wasim say when he greets Suraj's grandmother?
qa.a: He puts a hand on his chest and says “Assalamu alaikum.”

qa.q: What does Suraj feel about touching his grandfather's feet?
qa.a: It is his way of saying thank you, and he seems to value the blessing. He also comes to see that other ways of showing respect are just as good.

qa.q: What did the grandmother do that respected Wasim's choice?
qa.a: She asked “May I bless you too?” and waited for his nod before touching his head, and she accepted his greeting in his own way.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about being greeted by the grandmother in that way?
qa.a: Probably welcomed and respected, since she answered his greeting warmly and asked before touching him.

grounding: Touching elders' feet is a cultural sign of respect, and respect can be shown in other ways with consent.

passage: Note for staff, Teachers' Day. Kishore, Class 4. During the celebration, many children bent to touch my feet, as their families do with elders. It is a lovely custom. Kashish stood at the back, twisting her dupatta. A colleague nudged her forward: “Go on, touch Sir's feet.” Kashish's face tightened, and she stepped back. I said, “A namaste means just as much to me, Kashish.” She pressed her palms together and smiled properly for the first time that day. A reminder to all of us: children show respect in many ways, and no child should be pushed into touching anyone.

qa.q: What did Kashish twist while standing at the back?
qa.a: Kashish twisted her dupatta.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she was nudged forward?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable and reluctant, shown by her tightened face and stepping back; she may also simply have felt shy in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Kishore respect Kashish's choice?
qa.a: Kishore offered a namaste as an equally good way to show respect, so Kashish didn't have to touch anyone.

qa.q: How might the colleague who nudged her see the custom?
qa.a: The colleague probably saw touching feet as the proper way to show respect and didn't notice Kashish's discomfort.

grounding: Shows touching elders' feet as a respectful tradition, other ways of showing respect, and no child being pushed into unwanted touch.

passage: Saturday. Harsha's diary. Today was Leela Paati's eightieth birthday. When we reached her house, I bent down and touched her feet, like Amma taught me, and she put her hand on my head and said, “Nalla iru, kanna,” which means be well. Her hand was soft and shaky. I felt warm all over, like a blanket. My cousin Pranav, who lives in America, stood behind me looking confused. Later he asked me why. I said it's how we show respect and get blessings, but Paati is happy with a namaste too. He did a namaste, and Paati laughed and hugged him anyway.

qa.q: What did Leela Paati say to Harsha?
qa.a: She said, “Nalla iru, kanna,” which means be well.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel after Paati's blessing?
qa.a: Harsha felt warm and loved, like a blanket, from the touch of her soft hand.

qa.q: Which part of Harsha's explanation helped Pranav most?
qa.a: Saying that Paati is happy with a namaste too gave Pranav a comfortable way to show respect without copying a custom he didn't know.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Pranav?
qa.a: Pranav felt confused at first, then included when his namaste was welcomed with a laugh and a hug 😊

grounding: Shows a child touching an elder's feet to show respect and receive a blessing, and that respect can be shown in other ways too.

passage: At the wedding in their village near Jodhpur, the courtyard was full of relatives Preeti had never met. Her mother led her from elder to elder. Preeti bent and touched each pair of feet, quick and neat, and got pats on the head. Then a tall man with a big moustache, Lokesh-ji, a distant uncle, laughed and grabbed her wrist. “Come, come, touch properly, and give me a hug too.” Preeti's body went stiff, and she pulled back. Her mother stepped between them at once. “She has greeted you with respect, Lokesh-ji. A namaste is enough.” She kept Preeti beside her all evening and later told her, “You were right to pull back.”

qa.q: What did Lokesh-ji ask Preeti to give him besides touching his feet?
qa.a: He asked her to give him a hug too.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when her body went stiff?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and uneasy at being grabbed and asked for a hug by a man she didn't know.

qa.q: How did Preeti's mother protect her?
qa.a: She stepped between them at once, said a namaste was enough, kept Preeti beside her and told her she was right to pull back.

qa.q: How might the relatives nearby see her mother's words?
qa.a: Some might think she was being strict, but others would see a mother making sure respect never means unwanted touch.

grounding: Shows a child touching elders' feet as respect, and an adult making sure she is never forced into unwelcome touch.

passage:
When Nani arrived at the flat in Oslo, straight from the airport in her thick shawl, Amara bent and touched both of Nani's feet. Nani placed a hand on her head. "Jeete raho, my girl."

Lars, from next door, stared from the doorway. "Why do you touch her shoes?"

"It's respect," Amara said, "and she gives me a blessing back."

Amara's little cousin Pihu hid behind the sofa, shy of this new grandmother. "Pihu, touch Nani's feet," someone said. Amara's mother shook her head. "Only if she wants to. A namaste is respect too."

Pihu waved instead. Nani waved back, delighted. Lars shyly held out his hand, and Nani shook it.

qa.q: What did Nani place on Amara's head?
qa.a: Nani placed a hand on her head.

qa.q: What might Pihu have been feeling behind the sofa?
qa.a: Shy and a little uneasy with a grandmother she didn't know yet, which is why she hid and chose to wave instead.

qa.q: Which choice protected Pihu while still honouring Nani?
qa.a: Amara's mother said Pihu should only touch Nani's feet if she wanted to and that a namaste is respect too, so Pihu could greet her with a wave.

qa.q: How does Lars see the custom at first?
qa.a: Lars is puzzled and asks why Amara touches Nani's shoes; after Amara explains, he joins in his own way with a handshake.

grounding: It shows a child touching an elder's feet for respect and a blessing, while a younger child is not forced and greets her another way.
